adventist.great_apostasy:
Adventists speak of a falling away after the age of the apostles, not as the disappearance of every sincere believer, but as the church departing from plain Bible teaching. They point especially to the rise of Sunday in place of the seventh-day Sabbath, the mixing of church and civil power, and teachings about the immortal soul and eternal torment that they do not find in Scripture.

The falling away is read from passages such as 2 Thessalonians 2 and Revelation 12–13. Adventists do not usually say that God left the world without light. They hold that Scripture remained, that reformers recovered much truth, and that God still had people in many communions. The falling away names a long drift from apostolic practice that the Advent movement believes it was raised to help reverse.
adventist.restoration:
Adventists often call the last-day people of God a remnant. The word comes from Revelation 12:17: those who keep the commandments of God and have the testimony of Jesus. For most Adventists that means loyalty to all ten commandments, including the seventh-day Sabbath, and a recovery of neglected Bible truths about the sanctuary, the state of the dead, and the soon Advent.

Remnant does not mean that only one denomination contains every saved person. It names a visible last-day movement with a distinctive message. How tightly remnant is tied to one church body varies. Seventh-day Adventists commonly identify their own movement with that remnant calling. Other Adventist groups share the Advent hope and much of the same reading of prophecy while speaking of remnant in a broader or less institutional way.
adventist.foot_washing:
Many Adventist congregations practice the ordinance of humility, washing one another's feet before the Lord's Supper. They take the pattern from John 13, where Jesus washed the disciples' feet and told them to do as He had done. The act is treated as an ordinance of the church, not as a mere object lesson, and it is meant to express mutual service and the clearing of grudges before communion.

It is not viewed as a sacrament that confers grace by the rite itself. Participation is by believers. Some smaller Adventist bodies give the ordinance less emphasis or leave its frequency to the local congregation, but among Seventh-day Adventists it is a regular part of the communion service.
adventist.liturgical_calendar:
Adventists do not keep a church year of saints' days and prescribed seasons in the way liturgical churches do. The biblical feasts question is handled by asking what the Mosaic festivals meant and whether any of them remain binding as holy days. The near-universal Adventist answer is that those feasts were shadows that met their reality in Christ, so they are not required as annual observances.

The weekly seventh-day Sabbath is treated differently: it is read as part of the Ten Commandments, given at creation and not limited to the ceremonial law. Adventists mark Christmas or Easter only as local custom, if at all. A few Adventists study the typology of the feasts closely for prophecy, but that study is not the same as keeping a festal calendar as law.
adventist.sabbath:
Adventists keep the seventh-day Sabbath, from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset, as the day God blessed at creation and wrote into the Ten Commandments. They read Exodus 20 and the example of Jesus and the apostles as leaving the seventh day unchanged. Sunday is respected as a day many Christians gather, but it is not accepted as a transferred Sabbath.

Sabbath is for rest, worship, and mercy, not for earning salvation. How strictly work, cooking, or travel are limited varies by congregation and family. Seventh-day Adventists make the Sabbath a central mark of last-day loyalty. Some other Adventist groups historically kept Sunday or treated the day as secondary; the name Adventist in common use now almost always means seventh-day Sabbath keepers.
adventist.intermediate_state:
Adventists describe the state of the dead as a sleep until the resurrection. A person who dies does not go at once to the final reward or to conscious torment. Life depends on God; when breath leaves the body, thoughts perish until Christ calls the dead forth.

This reading is drawn from Ecclesiastes 9, the Psalms, and Jesus' words about Lazarus sleeping. It is meant to honor the resurrection as the real hope, not a soul that never dies. Adventists therefore do not pray to the dead or expect messages from them. Differences inside the wider Adventist family are small on this point; unconscious sleep until the Advent is one of the teachings that most Adventist bodies share.
adventist.soul_sleep:
Soul sleep is the Adventist name for the teaching that the dead are unconscious. Adventists do not hold that a person has an immortal soul that flies to heaven or hell at death. Soul in Scripture, as they read it, often means the living person. Immortality is a gift brought to light in the gospel and received at the resurrection of the just.

They reject spiritualism and any claim that the dead communicate with the living, treating such claims as deception. Conditional immortality hangs together with this: eternal life is not natural to the human being but granted by Christ. Almost all historic Adventist groups, including Seventh-day Adventists and Advent Christians, have taught soul sleep.
adventist.last_judgment:
Adventists expect a real judgment before the Second Coming, not only a public scene after it. In Seventh-day Adventist teaching this is the investigative judgment, begun in 1844 in the heavenly sanctuary, in which the lives of professed believers are reviewed before the universe while Christ ministers as high priest.

Not every Adventist body accepts that 1844 sanctuary reading. Advent Christian churches and some other Adventist groups hold a future judgment at Christ's return without a pre-Advent investigative phase in those terms. What the family shares is that judgment is God's, that it is according to works as evidence of faith, and that it is tied to the Advent hope rather than to an immediately conscious reward at death.
adventist.second_coming:
The Advent is the personal, visible, glorious return of Jesus. Adventists take their name from that hope. They teach that He comes in the clouds, that every eye will see Him, that the righteous dead are raised and the living righteous are caught up together with them, and that this event is near.

They do not treat the Advent as a secret coming for the church followed later by a public appearing. Date-setting after the 1844 disappointment is refused; watchfulness is not the same as naming the day. Emphasis falls on readiness, the commandments of God, and the gospel going to all the world before the end.
adventist.millennium:
Adventists generally teach a millennium of a thousand years that begins at the Second Coming. In the usual Seventh-day Adventist outline the righteous are taken to heaven with Christ, the earth lies desolate, the wicked remain dead, and Satan is bound by that very emptiness. At the close of the thousand years the wicked are raised, the New Jerusalem descends, final judgment is executed, and God makes a new earth.

This is neither a golden age of the church on earth before Christ returns nor a secret rapture that leaves ordinary history running. Some smaller Adventist groups describe the thousand years with less detail, but the family agrees that the millennium belongs to the Advent and resurrection, not to a merely political triumph of the church.
adventist.rapture:
Adventists reject a secret rapture that removes believers while the world goes on unaware. They read 1 Thessalonians 4 and Matthew 24 as one public coming: a shout, a trumpet, the dead in Christ rising, and the living caught up with them in sight of all. No secret rapture, as they use the phrase, means there are not two second comings or a hidden vanishing of the church years before the visible Advent.

Tribulation, in this reading, is faced by the last-day church on earth. The blessed hope is not escape from history in an unseen event but meeting the Lord in the air when He appears.
adventist.annihilation:
Adventists teach annihilation, or conditional immortality: the lost do not burn in conscious torment without end. After the final judgment the wicked perish. Malachi's image of ashes underfoot and the biblical words destroy, perish, and second death are taken in their ordinary sense.

God alone is said to have immortality in Himself; human beings receive immortality as a gift. Eternal punishment means a punishment whose result is eternal, not an everlasting process of pain. This is held as a teaching about God's justice and mercy together. It is shared across most Adventist bodies and is one of the points on which they have long differed from the majority Protestant tradition.
adventist.tithing:
Adventists commonly teach the tithe as one tenth of income returned to God for the support of gospel ministry. They read Malachi 3 and the Mosaic tithe as stating a principle that the New Testament does not cancel. Tithe is brought into the church storehouse; freewill offerings stand beside it for other work.

Tithe is not treated as a purchase of salvation. Practice is strong among Seventh-day Adventists, who channel tithe through conference structures to pay ministers. Other Adventist groups may be less centralized. Ability and conscience affect how strictly households apply the tenth, but the teaching itself is ordinary Adventist speech.
adventist.alcohol:
Temperance, for Adventists, means more than moderation in drink. The usual counsel is abstinence from alcohol, along with caution about tobacco and other intoxicants. The body is called the temple of the Holy Spirit; clouding the mind is treated as unfit for people who expect the Advent.

This stance grew with the nineteenth-century health reform that shaped the Adventist movement. It is strongest in Seventh-day Adventist official teaching. Individuals vary, and not every small Adventist body makes abstinence a test of fellowship, but temperance as abstinence rather than measured use is the native Adventist vocabulary.
adventist.food_laws:
The Adventist health message includes diet. Many Adventists avoid the meats labeled unclean in Leviticus 11, not as a path to justification but as wisdom that still teaches. A large share of Seventh-day Adventists go further toward vegetarian or plant-centered eating, following health-reform counsel that grew up with the movement.

The health message also covers rest, exercise, water, sunlight, and trust in God. It is not uniform in every Adventist household. Advent Christians have not always carried the same food rules. Where the health message is taught, it is framed as stewardship of the body while waiting for the Advent, not as a second gospel.
adventist.investigative_judgment:
Many Adventist bodies teach a pre-advent judgment: a judgment that takes place in heaven before Christ returns, distinct from the final judgment at the end of the age. It is usually connected with the prophecies of Daniel and with the Adventist movement's history in the 1840s, and it is often described as an examination of the records of all who have professed faith, showing whose faith is genuine.

Adventists who hold this teaching stress that it is meant as good news. Christ is the advocate and judge, and the judgment vindicates God's justice and those who trust in him, rather than aiming to frighten believers. The most fully developed form of the teaching is found in the Seventh-day Adventist Church. Not every Adventist group holds it in the same form, and some interpret the relevant prophecies differently.
